_display_rule: A month counts as 'cropped' if at least 15 of its days fall within a phase (computed on the 2025 reference year, wrapping across the year boundary).

Ben_Tre_DBSCL.salinity_months_source: Vĩnh Long (which now includes former Bến Tre): 'Stay especially alert from 2/2027 to 4/2027' (NAEC salinity handbook 2026–2027, p.50, translated from Vietnamese).

stress_years.event: 2016 drought and salinity intrusion: salt water reached about 93 km inland, the deepest recorded up to then.
stress_years.source: Ambio (2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8800995 (abstract read; full text not yet read)

stress_years.event: 2019–2020 drought and salinity intrusion: more severe than 2016 on all hydrological indicators.
stress_years.source: Ambio (2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8800995 (abstract read; full text not yet read)

Ben_Tre_DBSCL.stress_years_source: Crop year y = Summer-Autumn rice sown in year y + dry-season crop sown 1 Nov of year y; the 2016 and 2020 dry seasons fall in crop years 2015/16 and 2019/20.
Ben_Tre_DBSCL.ndvi_years_source: Period with a verified two-rice-crop calendar: MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI 2022–2024 at point 10.0992, 106.6040, and Báo Nông nghiệp Việt Nam [Vietnam Agriculture newspaper], 22/02/2024 ('only two rice crops a year', 'do not sow the 2023 Autumn–Winter crop'; translated from Vietnamese).
assumptions: Sowing dates are representative dates (Summer–Autumn rice 25 May, Winter–Spring rice 1 Nov); actual dates vary from year to year.

Extra water for rice follows FAO Training Manual 3 (1986), section 4.4: soil saturation 200 mm + standing water layer 100 mm + percolation 4 mm/day (heavy clay level). The soil type at Ba Tri is an assumed soil type, not yet verified. This extra water makes up most of the rice water need.

A water-balance study in Bến Tre uses a percolation rate of 2 mm/day, citing TCVN 9168:2012 (original standard not read). At 2 mm/day, the extra water for each 105-day rice crop is 510 mm instead of 720 mm.
The app has no station salinity data yet; salinity months come from published documents, not from measurements.
Weather comes from NASA POWER at the exact field coordinates (10.0992, 106.6040), but each value is the average of a grid cell of about 0.5° × 0.625° (roughly 50 km), not a measurement in the field.

Water deficit is summed month by month: a month with surplus rain does not offset a deficit month, because the model does not yet track water stored in the soil. Rice uses FAO TM3 effective rainfall (Pe = 0.8P − 25 when P > 75 mm/month; Pe = 0.6P − 10 when P < 75 mm/month); upland crops use USDA-SCS.

strategies.name_vi: Current practice: 2 rice crops (Summer–Autumn + early Winter–Spring)

phases.label: Early Winter–Spring rice
phases.presaturated_source: FAO TM3 section 4.4: soil saturation water (SAT) is not counted again when the root zone was already saturated in the previous month. The field has just gone through September–October, among the rainiest months of the year according to NASA POWER, so the Winter–Spring crop does not add the 200 mm for soil saturation.

strategies.why: This is how the field is farmed today; it is the baseline for comparison.

evidence.text: NDVI at point 10.0992, 106.6040 (2022–2024): two peaks each year (June–August and December–January), low from March to May.
evidence.source: NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 via ORNL DAAC

evidence.text: Mỹ Chánh commune, Ba Tri: 'only two rice crops a year'; farmers were urged 'not to sow the 2023 Autumn–Winter crop' (translated from Vietnamese).
evidence.source: Báo Nông nghiệp Việt Nam [Vietnam Agriculture newspaper], 22/02/2024

evidence.text: Coastal areas: 'finish all sowing within October to November (solar calendar) so as to harvest before salinity intrusion peaks' (translated from Vietnamese).

benefits: Avoids the February–April salinity peak, as recommended.
Farmers already know the techniques and the market.
info_gaps: Actual sowing dates in each year.
risks: The land lies bare in the dry season, which is also the salinity season: no ground cover and no income.
Late-sown Winter–Spring rice may meet salinity at the end of the season.

strategies.name_vi: Rice–shrimp (wet-season rice, tiger shrimp in the dry season)
strategies.why: Instead of fighting salinity, use dry-season brackish water to raise shrimp; grow rice once the rains have flushed out the salt.
strategies.note: The shrimp crop uses dry-season brackish water, so it is not counted as fresh water; the figures on this card cover the rice only (shrimp phase not modeled). 'Only sow rice when … soil salinity < 2‰' (NAEC salinity handbook 2026–2027, p.10, translated from Vietnamese).

evidence.text: Bình Đại (coastal district next to Ba Tri): 'Rice crop from 9/2012 to 12/2012… Tiger shrimp crop from 3/2013 to 7/2013.' (translated from Vietnamese)
evidence.source: Nguyễn Mỹ Hoa, Trần Sơn Tùng, Nguyễn Hồng Giang, Võ Thị Gương (2016). Tạp chí KH ĐH Cần Thơ [Can Tho University Journal of Science], Part A, 42: 40–49

evidence.text: Coastal Vĩnh Long: 'zone saline and brackish areas, do not rigidly convert them to fresh water; arrange livelihoods to suit the water source.' (translated from Vietnamese)

benefits: Income in the dry season instead of leaving the land bare.
Needs little fresh water in the dry season.

The rice crop helps flush salt from the soil: 'growing rice in rotation instead of intensive tiger shrimp farming flushed the salt out of the soil' (Nguyễn Mỹ Hoa et al., 2016, translated from Vietnamese).
info_gaps: No rice–shrimp calendar source specific to Ba Tri yet; the Bình Đại calendar is used.
The app does not yet model the water use and risks of the shrimp crop.
Investment cost, shrimp disease and market: farmers and extension officers need to assess these.
risks: During the shrimp crop, soil ESP was 20.7–25.4: 'the soil may reach the sodicity threshold' (Nguyễn Mỹ Hoa et al., 2016, translated from Vietnamese).
'Only sow rice when … soil salinity < 2‰' (NAEC, p.10, translated from Vietnamese): if the rains come late, the rice crop is easily damaged.
'Pause expanding the area in zones where on-farm irrigation infrastructure is not yet complete' (NAEC, p.10, translated from Vietnamese).

strategies.name_vi: Summer–Autumn rice + soybean instead of the Winter–Spring crop
strategies.why: Soybean does not need the land-preparation and percolation water of flooded rice, tolerates salinity better than maize, and is a nitrogen-fixing legume.

evidence.text: ECe threshold: soybean 5.0 dS/m; maize 1.7 dS/m.
Bến Tre has a policy supporting the conversion of rice land to upland crops: Decision 1353/QĐ-UBND of 11/07/2014.

Long Khánh commune, Cai Lậy, Tiền Giang (triple-rice land inside dikes, freshwater zone): after mung bean in the Summer–Autumn season, the following rice crop took up 98 kg N/ha from the soil, versus 69 kg N/ha in fields with three continuous rice crops; rice yield of the following crop was 4.6 t/ha, versus 3 t/ha. The test crop was mung bean, not soybean.
evidence.source: Võ Thị Gương, Nguyễn Minh Đông, Châu Minh Khôi (2010). Tạp chí Khoa học ĐH Cần Thơ [Can Tho University Journal of Science] 16b: 147–154, p.152

benefits: Lower fresh-water need than rice (see model figures).
Legume: rotation with rice increases the soil nitrogen available to the following rice crop (measured with mung bean in the freshwater zone of Tiền Giang).
info_gaps: Soybean sowing calendar on coastal Bến Tre rice land: no source found; the app assumes 1 Nov, 100 days.
Measurements for soybean on saline coastal rice land: none yet. The measurements used are for mung bean in Tiền Giang (freshwater zone).
Local market and price of soybean.
risks: Rice land waterlogs easily: raised beds and drainage are needed (local extension guidance required).
Late in the season (January–February) salinity starts to enter the rivers: irrigation water may be saline.
Farmers are not yet familiar with the techniques.

strategies.name_vi: Summer–Autumn rice + maize instead of the Winter–Spring crop
strategies.why: Maize does not need the land-preparation and percolation water of flooded rice; it can be used as animal feed.

evidence.text: Maize ECe threshold is 1.7 dS/m, the lowest of the compared crops.

Ba Tri, low-salinity sub-zone (4/2012–6/2013): a maize–rice–rice system was tested, together with watermelon–rice–rice and okra–rice–rice, against three rice crops. The okra–rice–rice system gave the highest economic return.
evidence.source: Nguyễn Mỹ Hoa et al. (2014). Tạp chí Khoa học ĐH Cần Thơ [Can Tho University Journal of Science], special issue on Agriculture: 31–37 (abstract)

evidence.text: Same experiment in Cai Lậy, Tiền Giang (freshwater zone): after baby corn, the following rice crop took up 105 kg N/ha, versus 69 kg N/ha in fields with three rice crops; yield 4.0 t/ha, versus 3 t/ha. The test crop was baby corn, not grain maize.
evidence.source: Võ Thị Gương, Nguyễn Minh Đông, Châu Minh Khôi (2010). Tạp chí Khoa học ĐH Cần Thơ [Can Tho University Journal of Science] 16b: 147–154, p.152

benefits: Lower fresh-water need than rice (see model figures).
Rotating an upland crop with rice raises the yield of the following rice crop (measured with baby corn in the freshwater zone of Tiền Giang).
info_gaps: Maize sowing calendar on coastal Bến Tre rice land: no source found; the app assumes 1 Nov, 100 days.
Local market and price of maize.
risks: Maize is very salt-sensitive: high risk if irrigation water turns saline late in the season.

assumptions: Coffee is assessed over January–April (dry season) with a fixed mid-season Kc.
There is no sourced daily heat threshold for Robusta coffee, so heat risk is not computed.

The FAO-56 water need is the full crop requirement. Vietnamese irrigation guidelines: 350–420 litres/tree/round, every 30–35 days (NAEC 2026); 500–520 litres/tree/round, every 30–40 days on basalt soil (WASI, Decision 26/QĐ-VNLT-KHKH 2013). At 1,111 trees/ha this is about 130–230 mm/season, lower than the model because of deliberate deficit irrigation and because basalt soil stores water from the rainy season (not yet modeled).

Weather comes from NASA POWER at the exact orchard coordinates (12.8314, 108.1282), but each value is the average of a grid cell of about 0.5° × 0.625° (roughly 50 km), not a measurement in the orchard.
Water deficit is summed month by month: a month with surplus rain does not offset a deficit month, because the model does not yet track water stored in the soil.

strategies.name_vi: Current practice: Robusta coffee on bare soil
strategies.why: This is how the orchard is farmed today; it is the baseline for comparison.

evidence.text: Kc for coffee on bare ground 0.90 / 0.95 / 0.95.
NDVI at point 12.8314, 108.1282 is high all year (about 0.66–0.80): a perennial crop.
evidence.source: NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 via ORNL DAAC

benefits: According to FAO-56, the dry-season water need is lower than for an orchard with grass cover.
info_gaps: Kc measured in the Central Highlands: no source yet.
risks: Bare soil loses water easily and erodes on slopes.
Robusta coffee is heat-sensitive: each 1 °C rise in the growing-season mean temperature reduces yield by about 14% (Kath et al., 2020, Global Change Biology).

strategies.name_vi: Robusta coffee with cover crop / grass cover
strategies.why: Extension services recommend 'planting ground-cover crops' and erosion control on slopes (translated from Vietnamese).
strategies.note: According to FAO-56, a full live grass cover increases water need, so the D1 figures are an upper bound. WASI guideline (Decision 26/QĐ-VNLT-KHKH, 2013): weed in strips on slopes, clear weeds around the orchard at the start of the dry season to prevent fire, mulch and add green manure at the end of the rainy season. No measurements from the Central Highlands were found showing that cover crops reduce irrigation water.

evidence.text: 'Strengthen the system of shade trees and windbreaks, plant ground-cover crops…'; 'On slopes, lay out trenches, strips or water-catchment pits along contour lines to increase water retention and limit surface runoff and erosion.' (translated from Vietnamese)
evidence.source: National Agricultural Extension Center (NAEC), coffee and pepper drought and salinity leaflet (2026)

evidence.text: WASI guideline: 'clear weeds 3–4 times/year'; 'On slopes: weed in strips, do not clear-weed the whole area'; at the start of the dry season 'clear weeds around the coffee orchard to prevent fire'; at the end of the rainy season 'mulch the base, add green manure'. (translated from Vietnamese)
evidence.source: WASI, ICM guideline for Robusta coffee in the bearing stage, Decision 26/QĐ-VNLT-KHKH of 04/3/2013

benefits: Covers the soil, limiting surface runoff and erosion.
May increase soil organic matter (needs on-site measurement).
info_gaps: No measurements yet from the Central Highlands on how cover crops affect irrigation need; FAO-56 assumes grass increases ETc.
Suitable cover-crop species and how to manage them in the dry season.
risks: Cover crops may compete with coffee for water in the dry season (see model figures).
Managing cover crops in the dry season (cutting, mulching) needs guidance from local experts.

The WASI guideline does not recommend keeping a full grass cover over the orchard in the dry season; it recommends weeding in strips. The FAO-56 'with weeds' Kc assumes full grass cover, so the D1 figures are an upper bound of water need.
